title: Arthritis, leaving Whiteman and the diet that eased it
summary: Whiteman had him play solos; pain in his fingers was diagnosed as arthritis; he changed diet and regained some use but quit playing.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: And I didn't expect to be so successful, so successful with music. After laying off it for so long, for seven years you may as well say, and then returning to it, and start playing and working my way up from, I was just stepping from one office to the other. Better orchestra, and better orchestra, and more money, and more money up until I time to get the Whiteman. When I got the Whiteman, I figured, well, I can't go any further. So, that was a time when I'd get out and play before the band. Whiteman used to make me come out in the front, play a solo. And, in grabbing the strings, my arm used to pain me awful, and I didn't know what was happening. My fingers were feeling bad, and I didn't know what it was. But anyway, after I left Whiteman, I went to the hospital and had them take an x-ray of my fingers, thinking I had a fractured bone or something that was aching me so. And the doctors told me, oh, it was arthritis. And they told me, I asked them what they could do. They said, well, we can't tell you. There's not a cure known for it.
So, up to date, there's not a cure known for it.

So, I read a book one time, and it says that the only thing they could advise a person to do, that any sickness is caused by what a person eats. So, they advised me to go on a diet, a quick diet, and just change around.
Let me answer, I think that's Ralph. Go ahead.

They thought that the best thing to do would be to replace things of what I had been doing. So, I quit drinking coffee, I quit drinking any sort of liquors, and I quit eating meats of any kind. Nothing but vegetables, nothing but barley coffee, and things like that. And I've done that for about four years. And my fingers commenced to limber up. And I think that's what it largely did. That's five o'clock, isn't it?
Yeah, it's about five. It is. Two minutes to five.

Then, in conjunction with that, I took what they call Neutrolite, and that seemed to help me a whole lot, too. Sort of a vitamin. Oh, I see. And then later on, I started eating meat again. And so far, I've been able to navigate around. But my fingers are not so that I could finger a bass like I'd want to. I can bluff things around a while. And maybe as old as I am, I'm going to be like Tom a little later on, grab a hold of a bass all of a sudden, you know, and sit in with a band and start playing again. But it'll never be anything like I used to do.
Well, you can still do it better, as I say, and better than...
Well, that's what a lot of musicians said, but my playing didn't satisfy me, and because it didn't satisfy me, why I tried to do something else, you know.
